column4: God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, joining the palace greeting for the follower of guidance to its final destination.
The children of Adam are reminded of God's covenant not to serve Satan, the clear enemy, placing the warning before the divided path.
Serving God is identified as the straight path, making the response to warning a road rather than an abstract assent.
Satan has led many generations astray, a broad counterpart to the companion who nearly draws the believer into ruin.
The warned are shown the Hell they were promised, bringing promise, warning, and fire to the point of encounter.
They are commanded to enter and burn in it because they denied, directly joining denial to entry into the warning-fire.
God makes a way out for whoever has taqwa, giving the section's protective fear a literal opening in the road.
He provides from an unexpected direction and suffices the one who trusts Him, while setting a measure for everything; provision, true sufficiency, and measure meet here.
The audience is told to race toward forgiveness and a vast garden prepared for those with taqwa, joining urgent movement, shield, and garden.
The people of taqwa spend in prosperity and adversity, restrain anger, and pardon, specifying the giving conduct that leads to that garden.
The people of the garden receive what their Lord gives them because they previously did good, reversing the direction of giving at the garden's reward.
Within their wealth is an acknowledged right for the asker and deprived, making the giving hand part of the conduct that precedes the garden.
The one who brings truth and the one who confirms it are identified as the people of taqwa, joining affirmation to the section's protective stance.
They have whatever they desire with their Lord, and that is the reward of those who do good, carrying affirmation and taqwa into divine recompense.
Those who are stingy, command stinginess, and conceal what God gave from His bounty combine the clenched hand with denial of the original Giver.
The hypocrites command wrong, forbid right, and close their hands; forgetting God follows the same bodily posture of refusal the section gives to the miser.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither wastefully nor stingily but hold a measured course, giving the opened hand a disciplined middle position.
Those who pray and spend secretly and openly hope for a trade that will never perish, directing transient wealth toward what remains.
God fully repays them and increases them from His bounty, joining recompense and increase to the giving that sought an imperishable return.
The hypocrites urge others to stop spending on the Messenger's companions so they disperse, although the treasuries of heaven and earth belong to God; withholding confronts divine ownership.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children turn them from God's remembrance, identifying possession itself as a possible agent of turning.
They are told to spend before death makes a person beg for time to give charity and become righteous, showing the giving hand recognized too late.
When the human receives expansive provision, he calls it his Lord's honoring, exposing the mistaken equation of received wealth with true elevation.
When provision is measured tightly, he calls it humiliation; the following failures toward orphan and needy show why wealth is not the measure of height.
God purchases believers' lives and wealth in exchange for the garden and names His promise true, uniting wealth given away, divine covenant, and garden return.
Qarun exalts himself over Moses' people while treasure keys burden a strong company, staging wealth as both claimed height and physical weight.
He is told to seek the final abode with what God gave him, do good as God did good to him, and avoid corruption, directing received wealth toward its Giver and the last life.
Qarun claims he received his wealth because of knowledge he possesses, replacing divine bounty with self-sufficient possession even after stronger wealthy peoples were destroyed.
He comes out in adornment and those desiring the near life wish for wealth like his, showing possession attracting faces toward worldly height.
Those given knowledge answer that God's reward is better for believers who do right, redirecting desire from displayed wealth toward the lasting return.
God makes the earth swallow Qarun and his house; no company helps him against God and he cannot save himself, an exceptionally close meeting of wealth, fall, absent hand, and ruin.
Those who had desired Qarun's place recognize that God expands and measures provision and that His favor kept them from being swallowed, turning envy into acknowledgment of saving bounty.
The garden owner boasts to his believing companion that he has more wealth and a stronger following, joining possession, social power, and companionship.
He enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, treating fertile possession as permanent support.
He doubts the Hour and assumes that even if returned to his Lord he will find a better resort, making denial and self-sufficiency speak inside the garden.
His companion answers by recalling the God who created him from dust and a drop, confronting denial with the Creator just as Moses confronts Pharaoh.
The believer declares God his Lord and refuses to associate anyone with Him, providing the companion's affirmation against the owner's boast.
He tells the owner to acknowledge God's will and that power belongs only to God when entering the garden, locating the true supporting hand over the apparent wealth.
The believer warns that his Lord may give him a better garden and send a calamity that turns the other's garden into barren ground, bringing divine giving and garden reversal together.
He warns that its water may sink beyond recovery, making the garden's apparent provision fall out of the owner's reach.
The mocking companion asks whether dust and bones will really be judged after death, specifying the denial recalled in 37:52 before the downward look into Hell.
At the fire the voice identifies itself as Moses' Lord and marks the valley as sacred, confirming that the approached flame is the site of divine address.
God tells Moses that he has been chosen and must listen to revelation, giving the night-fire its guiding function through heard speech.
The speaker at the fire declares Himself God and commands worship and remembrance, fixing the true Lord before Moses later faces Pharaoh's competing claim.
The voice at the fire tells Moses that it is God, the Mighty and Wise, explicitly identifying the giver of the sign and guidance.
Moses offers Pharaoh a path to purification, placing the cleansing movement later associated with giving inside the royal confrontation.
He offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he will fear, joining guidance and protective fear in the rejected palace message.
Moses shows Pharaoh the greatest sign, identifying what Pharaoh denies in the next ayah rather than leaving his denial objectless.
God sends Moses and Aaron together to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, establishing the two messengers and the king in the palace encounter.
They are commanded to speak gently so Pharaoh may remember or fear, showing that the warning seeks the very fear that would protect him.
The two confess fear that Pharaoh will hasten against them or transgress further, making royal force part of the confrontation with divine guidance.
God tells them not to fear because He is with them hearing and seeing, supplying the divine support beneath the hands sent before the king.
God guides Moses to lead His servants by night and strike a dry path through the sea without fear of pursuit or drowning, turning guidance into a safe road at the edge of destruction.
Pharaoh follows with his forces and the sea overwhelms them, giving the self-exalting king the downward outcome avoided by the guided walkers.
Pharaoh is judged to have led his people astray rather than guided them, directly opposing the holding king's leadership to the Lord who gives and guides.
God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea, bringing the claimant of height under the stronger divine taking hand.
Pharaoh makes light of his people and they obey him, showing how the king's claimed elevation draws others onto his course.
When they provoke God's anger He takes retribution and drowns them all, completing the fall beneath the king's earlier boast over rivers.
Pharaoh orders Haman to build him a tower so he may reach the ways, turning the king's claim of height into an attempted structure.
He says he will ascend toward Moses' God while calling Moses a liar, and his scheme bars him from the path and ends in ruin; height, denial, path, and collapse meet here.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to fire morning and evening and then ordered into harsher punishment when the Hour comes, fixing the final fire beneath their worldly elevation.
The dominion of everything is in God's hand and all are returned to Him, a direct answer to every human attempt to hold wealth or kingdom.
On resurrection the whole earth is in God's grasp and the heavens folded in His right hand, making the supporting and possessing divine hand cosmic in scope.
The Messenger asks no payment for warning except that a person choose a path to the Lord, joining refusal of return to the road the hearer takes.
Faces on that Day are radiant, directly continuing the section's movement from covered night and frowning day to disclosed face.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, placing the face's final direction upon the Lord whose face was sought in giving.
Some faces on that Day are bright, another direct formulation of the face opened after the protected course.
Those faces laugh and rejoice, giving emotional content to the final satisfaction promised after striving.
Other faces have dust upon them, reversing radiance with a covering that recalls the road ending in descent.
Darkness covers those faces, making the covering night a judgment image for disbelief rather than the setting through which guidance was read.
The contented soul is directly addressed, giving the section's final رضى an inward bearer.
It returns to its Lord pleased and pleasing, joining return, mutual approval, and the Lord toward whom the face was directed.
It is invited among God's servants, the saved company opposite the companion found in Hell.
It is invited into God's garden, placing satisfaction at the entrance to the garden-side outcome.
Enduring gardens, God's pleasure with the faithful and theirs with Him, and fear of the Lord all meet in one reward, tightly joining رضى, garden, and protective fear.
The command is to remind wherever reminder benefits, introducing the warning that separates the hearers in the following ayat.
The one who fears will take the reminder, tying responsiveness to the fear that keeps a person from fire.
The most wretched person avoids the reminder, the exact contrary course of the hearer who turns aside from the fire itself.
That wretched person enters the greatest fire, directly linking refusal of warning to entry into flame.
Within it he neither dies nor lives, specifying the condition reached by the one who entered rather than read the fire as a sign.
Success belongs to the one who purifies himself, corresponding to wealth given in order to grow in purity.
He remembers his Lord's name and prays, giving the successful course its orientation toward the Lord Most High.
People instead prefer the nearer life, naming the temporal preference behind clutched wealth and worldly royal height.
The Hereafter is better and more enduring, explaining why wealth and rule cannot support their owner at the fall.
Those who disbelieve in their Lord receive Hell, the evil destination that begins the surah's warning interrogation.
When cast into it they hear it roaring as it boils, making entry into fire the opposite of hearing guidance beside Moses' fire.
Hell's keepers ask each arriving company whether a warner came to them, centering the scene on their treatment of warning.
They admit that a warner came but they denied him, directly explaining why the warning-fire became the entered fire.
They say that listening or reasoning would have kept them from being companions of the blaze, defining the missed act at the sign.
They confess their sin, completing their recognition from within the fire after warning could no longer redirect them.
Those who fear their Lord unseen receive forgiveness and great reward, providing the protected counterpart to those who only recognize the fire after entry.
The human being is laboring toward the Lord and will meet Him, directing all striving toward an unavoidable encounter.
The person given his record in his right hand begins the eased outcome of that striving.
He receives an easy accounting, an eschatological counterpart to being eased toward ease.
He returns to his people rejoicing, giving successful striving a satisfied social home.
The other person receives his record behind his back, making the turned back the bodily sign of the contrary outcome.
He calls for destruction, recognizing ruin only after taking the back-facing course.
He enters a blaze, completing the sequence from record behind the back to fire.
He had thought he would never return, identifying denial beneath his former ease among his family.
His Lord had always seen him, answering the illusion that his worldly course escaped the final return.
The person whose scales are heavy begins the secure outcome of measured striving.
He is in a pleasing life, joining moral weight to رضى rather than to the weight of possessions.
The person whose scales are light begins the reversed outcome, where apparent worldly weight proves empty.
His refuge is an abyss, a direct counterpart to the section's cliff and downward fall.
The abyss is identified as a fiercely hot fire, joining fall and fire in the shortest possible sequence.

Whoever seeks the harvest of the Hereafter receives increase in it, while one seeking the worldly harvest receives some of it but no share later; desire, growth, and first-last choice divide one ayah.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and then reaches Hell condemned, making divine giving itself no proof of final height.
Whoever wants the Hereafter, strives for it properly, and believes has that striving thanked, joining direction of desire to the value of effort.
God supplies both groups from His giving and His giving is not confined, establishing the open divine hand before the roads reach different ends.
Worldly ranks differ, but the Hereafter has greater degrees and preference, relocating true elevation beyond present possessions.
The fire just described is declared one of the greatest signs, explicitly making fire itself a sign rather than only a destination.
It is a warning to humanity, closely matching the section's warning-fire read as a signal.
The warning addresses whoever chooses to advance or fall back, turning response to the fire-sign into opposed movements.
The hearers are asked where they are going, forcing attention onto the direction of their course.
The revelation is declared a reminder to all peoples, identifying what can redirect that course.
The reminder is for whoever wills to take a straight course, directly joining warning and road.
Human willing remains under the will of God, Lord of all worlds, returning the walker's road to divine sovereignty.
Those who deny God's signs and act arrogantly cannot enter the garden, an impossible ascent image that bars self-exaltation from the high garden.
East and west belong to God and whichever way people turn there is God's face, setting a divine boundary around the merely directional turning rejected as righteousness in 2:177.
The kindled fire is closed over the wealth-counter and his kind, reversing the open road and matching the enclosed fire at the end of the steep-path passage.
Its extended columns specify the enclosure's structure, completing the fate of the person who treated accumulated wealth as support.
God is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, adding divine permanence and disclosed-hidden polarity to His ownership of the first and later life.
The garden-dwellers praise God for guiding them there and say they could not have found guidance without Him, carrying divine guidance to the garden outcome.
Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty, identifying the competing promises behind a hand that either closes or gives.
